comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C19-C27 regarding in vivo hypoxia model characterization, behavioral deficits, and histological damage. Both evaluations find the experimental design solid with appropriate controls and no methodological concerns.

Strong agreement on claims C28-C32 regarding snRNA-seq findings. OpenEval emphasizes bioinformatic rigor while peer reviewers praise the 'multi-omics combined analysis' approach. Peer review additionally addresses C2, C95, C96 in this grouping, showing broader integration of sequencing methodology claims.

Agreement on EV characterization and transcriptomic analysis (C33-C44). OpenEval notes minor interpretive extensions in C42-C43 but still supports overall. Peer review groups additional claims C45-C50 (cellular origin identification) with EV characterization, showing broader integration of EV-related findings.

Both support CIBERSORTx deconvolution findings (C45-C50, C96) for identifying EV cellular origins. OpenEval treats this as separate analysis while peer reviewers integrate it with broader EV characterization. Both acknowledge the computational approach as valid without raising methodological concerns.

Perfect agreement on claims C51-C56, C60 regarding hemoglobin protein accumulation in neurons and the inference of EV-mediated mRNA transfer. Both evaluations find the multi-modal evidence (sequencing, RT-qPCR, western blot, immunofluorescence) convincing for the intercellular transfer mechanism.

Agreement on mitochondrial dysfunction findings (C57-C59). OpenEval focuses specifically on these claims while peer review groups them with C44 (pathway enrichment). Both find the western blot and enzymatic activity data convincing without methodological concerns.

Perfect agreement on claims C61-C72 regarding in vitro hypoxia model establishment and cell-type-specific responses. Both evaluations find the time-course experiments with multiple complementary assays well-designed and the 8-hour timepoint selection well-justified.

Perfect agreement on claims C73-C87 regarding protective effects of conditioned medium transfer. Both evaluations find the systematic experiments across multiple neuronal models convincing. Peer reviewers explicitly praise the novelty of hemoglobin's mitochondrial protective function.

Perfect agreement on claims C88-C93 regarding loss-of-function experiments (EV depletion and HBA1 knockdown). Both evaluations find these critical controls provide strong evidence for the specific role of EV-carried HBA1 mRNA in the protective mechanism.

Disagreement on main conclusions (C3-C5, C100-C101, C104-C105). OpenEval supports the convergence of evidence for the CNS-specific mechanism. Peer reviewers raise critical concern about whole-body hypoxia model potentially introducing confounding systemic factors, creating uncertainty about whether CNS-specific EV transfer is the primary mechanism in vivo.

Perfect agreement on claims C102-C103 as UNCERTAIN. Both evaluations recognize these as explicit speculation by authors to reconcile in vivo damage with in vitro protection, lacking experimental validation in the current study.

OpenEval evaluated neuroglobin control analysis (C106) as supported, finding it strengthens the specificity of hemoglobin's role. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific control experiment.

Peer reviewers specifically evaluated the whole-body hypoxia model choice (C97) as introducing uncertainty due to potential systemic confounding factors. OpenEval did not separately evaluate this methodological limitation claim, though it may be implicit in the overall assessment.
